t.6.57.1: Having heard the evil-souled Rāvaṇa lamenting thus, tormented by grief, Triśiras spoke these words.
t.6.57.2: Just so, father, our mighty middle one has been slain. But good men do not lament as you do, O king.
t.6.57.3: Surely, O lord, you are a match even for the three worlds; why then, like an ordinary man, do you give yourself over to grief in this way?
t.6.57.4: You possess a spear granted by Brahmā, armor, an arrow and a bow, and a chariot yoked with a thousand donkeys whose rumble is like that of a thundercloud.
t.6.57.6: Stay here at your ease, great king; I will go forth to battle. I will root out your enemies here, as Garuḍa carries off serpents.
t.6.57.5: Time and again, even without a weapon, you have cut down gods and Dānavas; so now, equipped with every weapon, you ought to punish Rāghava.
t.6.57.7: Just as Śambara was struck down by the king of the gods, and Naraka by Viṣṇu, so today Rāma, felled by me in battle, will lie upon the ground.
t.6.57.8: Having heard the words of Triśiras, Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, driven on by Time, thought of himself as if born anew.
t.6.57.9: Having heard the words of Triśiras, Devāntaka and Narāntaka, and the splendid Atikāya too, became thrilled at the prospect of battle.
t.6.57.10: Then the heroic sons of Rāvaṇa, bulls among the Nairṛtas, equal to Śakra in valor, roared thus, each crying, "I, I!"
t.6.57.11: All of them roamed the sky, all were skilled in magic arts, all were crushers of the pride of the thirty gods, and all were mad with the frenzy of battle.
t.6.57.12: All were endowed with the strength of weapons, all were of widespread fame; all of them, having entered battle, were never heard to have been defeated.
t.6.57.13: All were heroes skilled in weapons, all were expert in warfare, all possessed excellent understanding, and all had likewise obtained boons.
t.6.57.14: Surrounded thus by those sons, radiant as the sun and crushers of the enemy's forces, the king shone forth as Maghavān shines when surrounded by the immortals, the destroyers of the pride of the great Dānavas.
t.6.57.15: Having embraced his sons and adorned them with ornaments, he sent them forth into battle with excellent blessings.
t.6.57.16: Rāvaṇa also sent the two brothers Mahodara and Mahāpārśva into battle for the protection of the princes.
t.6.57.17: Those huge-bodied ones, having saluted the great-souled Rāvaṇa, who makes his enemies cry out, and having circumambulated him reverently, set forth.
t.6.57.18: Having anointed themselves with all kinds of herbs and with perfumes, these six mighty ones, the foremost of the Nairṛtas, eager for battle, went forth.
t.6.57.19: Then Mahodara mounted the elephant named Sudarśana, which resembled a dark rain cloud and was born in the line of Airāvata.
t.6.57.20: Mounted upon an elephant equipped with every kind of weapon and well adorned with quivers, he shone like the sun upon the summit of the western mountain.
t.6.57.21: Triśiras, the son of Rāvaṇa, mounted a most excellent chariot yoked with the finest horses and filled with every kind of weapon.
t.6.57.22: Triśirā, the bowman, mounted upon his chariot, shone like a rain-cloud with lightning, meteors, flames and the rainbow of Indra.
t.6.57.23: With his three diadems, Triśiras shone forth upon that finest of chariots, like Himavān, lord of mountains, with its three golden peaks.
t.6.57.24: Then Atikāya too, the radiant son of the lord of the rākṣasas, foremost among all bowmen, mounted the finest of chariots.
t.6.57.25: A chariot with excellent wheels and axles, well harnessed, fitted with its under-frame and its pole, blazing with quivers and bows, and crowded with darts, swords and iron clubs.
t.6.57.26: With his resplendent diadem, wrought variously with gold, and with his ornaments, he shone like Meru, brilliant with its radiance.
t.6.57.27: That mighty son of the king shone forth upon that chariot, surrounded by tigers among the Nairṛtas, like Vajrapāṇi surrounded by the immortals.
t.6.57.28: Narāntaka mounted a horse resembling Uccaiḥśravas, white, adorned with gold, swift as thought and of enormous body.
t.6.57.29: Grasping a lance that blazed like a meteor, Narāntaka shone forth, like the splendid Guha who, having taken up his spear, shines among his foes in battle.
t.6.57.30: Devāntaka, taking up an iron club adorned with diamonds and grasping a mountain with his arms, appeared as if mimicking the form of Viṣṇu.
t.6.57.31: The mighty Mahāpārśva, of great splendour, taking up his mace, shone in battle, mace in hand, like Kubera.
t.6.57.32: Those great-souled ones set out, surrounded by matchless forces, like the gods in Amarāvatī surrounded by matchless hosts.
t.6.57.33: The great-souled Rākṣasas, bearing excellent weapons, followed them on elephants, on horses, and in chariots that rumbled like thunderclouds.
t.6.57.34: Those great-souled princes, radiant as the sun, crowned and endowed with splendour, shone forth like blazing planets in the sky.
t.6.57.35: The white row of their parasols, held aloft, shone like autumn clouds, like a line of swans in the sky.
t.6.57.36: Having resolved upon either death or the defeat of their enemies, and having thus made up their minds, the heroes, eager for battle, sallied forth.
t.6.57.37: As they marched forth, those mighty ones, mad for battle, roared and bellowed, loosed their arrows, and exulted.
t.6.57.38: With the sounds of their war-cries and the slapping of their arms, the earth seemed to tremble, and with the lion-like roars of the Rākṣasas the sky then seemed to split apart.
t.6.57.39: Having sallied forth, those mighty lords of the Rākṣasas, filled with joy, beheld the army of the Vānaras, its rocks and trees raised aloft.
t.6.57.40: The great-souled monkeys, too, beheld the army of the Nairṛtas, crowded with elephants, horses and chariots and resounding with hundreds of little bells.
t.6.57.41: Resembling a dark rain-cloud, with mighty weapons raised aloft, it was surrounded on all sides by Nairṛtas who shone like blazing fire and the sun.
t.6.57.42: Seeing that army approaching, the monkeys, who had found their target, raised mighty boulders and roared again and again.
t.6.57.43: Then, hearing the loud clamour raised by the leaders of the monkey troops, the mighty hosts of rākṣasas, unable to bear the fierce exultation of their foes, roared out still more terribly.
t.6.57.44: Those leaders of the monkey troops, having entered the dreadful army of the rākṣasas, roamed about with uplifted rocks, like peaked mountains.
t.6.57.45: Some of the monkeys, having entered the sky, and some on the earth, enraged, ranged among the armies of the Rākṣasas, armed with trees and rocks.
t.6.57.46: Though held back by floods of arrows, those monkeys of terrible prowess made an unsurpassed shower of trees, rocks and mountain peaks.
t.6.57.47: On the battlefield the rākṣasas and the vānaras roared lion-like roars, and the plavaṃgamas crushed the yātudhānas with rocks.
t.6.57.48: Some, enraged in the battle, struck down heroes clad in armor and ornaments, those mounted on chariots as well as those riding elephants and horses.
t.6.57.50: Then, in a moment, the earth became covered with rocks and swords hurled by the monkeys and rākṣasas, and was drenched with blood.
t.6.57.49: Leaping up suddenly, the monkeys struck down the yātudhānas with hurled mountain peaks or with their fists; and there the foremost of the rākṣasas, their eyes destroyed, reeled, fell, and cried out.
t.6.57.52: Those night-rangers struck down monkeys with monkeys themselves, and the monkeys too struck down rākṣasas with rākṣasas themselves.
t.6.57.51: With the rākṣasas, crushers of foes, lying about like scattered mountains, they were struck down and were being hurled about, their spears shattered by the monkeys.
t.6.57.53: Snatching away their rocks, the Rākṣasas struck down the monkeys; and the Vānaras, wresting their weapons from them, struck down the Rākṣasas.
t.6.57.54: In the battle the monkeys and rākṣasas struck one another with rocks, spears and missiles and tore one another apart, and they roared lion-like roars.
t.6.57.55: The rākṣasas, their armor and body-guards cut to pieces, were struck down by the monkeys, and there they streamed blood as trees exude their rich sap.
t.6.57.56: In the battle, some of the monkeys struck down chariot with chariot, elephant with elephant, and horse with horse.
t.6.57.57: With razor-edged arrows, crescent-headed arrows, broad-tipped bhalla arrows and other sharpened shafts, the Rākṣasas cut to pieces the trees and rocks of the chiefs of the Vānaras.
t.6.57.58: With scattered mountain peaks, with trees cut down in the battle, and with slain monkeys and rākṣasas, the earth became impassable.
t.6.57.59: When that tumultuous clash had begun, as the monkeys rejoiced and the rākṣasas were being struck down, the great sages and the hosts of gods cried out aloud.
t.6.57.60: Then Narāntaka, mounting a horse swift as the wind and seizing a sharpened spear, plunged into the army of the king of the monkeys as a fish enters the great ocean.
t.6.57.61: That hero pierced seven hundred monkeys with his blazing spear. Single-handed, in a moment, the great-souled enemy of Indra slaughtered the army of those bulls among monkeys.
t.6.57.62: And the Vidyādharas and great sages saw that mighty one, mounted on horseback, ranging among the armies of the monkeys.
t.6.57.63: His path was seen to be a mire of flesh and blood, strewn all over with fallen monkeys who looked like mountains.
t.6.57.64: Even as the bulls among the monkeys were making up their minds to advance, Narāntaka overran them and pierced them through.
t.6.57.65: Raising his blazing spear in the thick of the battle, Narāntaka burned up the monkey hosts as fire consumes the forests.
t.6.57.66: Even as the forest-dwellers were tearing up trees and rocks, they fell, struck down by darts, like mountains cleft by the thunderbolt.
t.6.57.67: The mighty Narāntaka ranged through all the directions in battle, crushing the foe on every side, like the wind in the rainy season.
t.6.57.68: The heroes could neither run nor stand still, much less stir; whether one leapt up, stood still or moved away, the mighty one pierced them all.
t.6.57.69: Pierced by a single lance that was like Antaka, Death himself, and blazing with the radiance of the sun, the hosts of monkeys fell down upon the surface of the earth.
t.6.57.70: The monkeys could not withstand the descent of the lance, which was like the crushing blow of a thunderbolt, and they cried out with a mighty roar.
t.6.57.71: The forms of the falling monkey heroes appeared like mountains whose lofty peaks had been shattered by the thunderbolt, falling down.
t.6.57.72: But those great-souled foremost of the vānaras who had earlier been struck down by Kumbhakarṇa, still unwell, came and stood before Sugrīva.
t.6.57.73: Looking around, Sugrīva saw the army of monkeys, terrified by fear of Narāntaka, fleeing hither and thither.
t.6.57.74: Seeing the army put to flight, he beheld Narāntaka approaching, lance in hand, mounted on the back of a horse.
t.6.57.75: Then Sugrīva of great splendour, lord of the monkeys, spoke to the heroic prince Aṅgada, whose valour equalled that of Śakra.
t.6.57.76: Go, O hero, against this rākṣasa who sits mounted on a horse, throwing the monkey army into turmoil, and swiftly part him from his life-breaths.
t.6.57.77: Having heard the words of his lord, Aṅgada then sprang forth from the army that resembled a mass of clouds, like the radiant sun emerging from a bank of clouds.
t.6.57.78: Aṅgada, the foremost of the monkeys, resembling a mass of rocks, shone girt with armlets, like a mountain streaked with mineral ores.
t.6.57.79: Weaponless, the greatly splendid son of Vālin, armed only with his nails and teeth, advanced toward Narāntaka and spoke these words.
t.6.57.80: Stop! What will you accomplish with these common monkeys? Hurl your spear at this chest of mine, whose touch is like the thunderbolt.
t.6.57.81: Hearing the words of Aṅgada, Narāntaka flew into a rage; biting his lip with his teeth, he hissed like a serpent.
t.6.57.82: Then, whirling a blazing spear, he suddenly hurled it at Aṅgada. That spear, striking the thunderbolt-like chest of Vālin's son, was shattered and fell to the ground.
t.6.57.83: Then, seeing that lance shattered like the body of a serpent cut apart by Suparṇa, the son of Vālin raised his palm and struck the horse upon its head.
t.6.57.84: Struck by a blow of the palm, his head shattered, his horse, huge as a mountain, fell to the ground, its legs sunk in, its eyeballs burst, its tongue hanging out.
t.6.57.85: Seeing his horse slain and fallen, Narāntaka was overcome by fury; that one of great might raised his fist and struck the son of Vālin on the head in battle.
t.6.57.86: Then Aṅgada, his head split open by the blow of the fist, poured forth a sharp stream of exceedingly hot blood; again and again he blazed up and swooned, and on regaining consciousness he was filled with amazement.
t.6.57.87: Then the great-souled Aṅgada, son of Vālin, clenching his fist, which was like a mountain peak and swift as the thunderbolt, brought it down upon the chest of Narāntaka.
t.6.57.88: His chest crushed and shattered by the blow of the fist, vomiting flame, his limbs smeared with blood, Narāntaka fell to the surface of the earth like a mountain shattered by the stroke of a thunderbolt.
t.6.57.89: Then, when that foremost hero Narāntaka had been slain in battle by the son of Vālin, a great roar arose from the best of the gods in the sky and from the forest-dwellers as well.
t.6.57.90: Then Aṅgada performed that most difficult feat of valor, which delighted the heart of Rāma. He too, of surpassing might and prowess, was astonished, and once more he grew joyful in battle.
